analysis.one_liner: Raises the bar for holding parent companies responsible for labor abuses at franchise and contract workplaces.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have raised the bar for holding parent companies responsible for franchise and contract workers' labor rights, was introduced in March 2016, received a committee hearing in June 2016, and never got a Senate vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change the National Labor Relations Act so that two companies (say, a fast-food corporation and its franchisee) are only considered "joint employers" if each directly and immediately controls the workers' essential employment terms [S2][S3]. Under the standard in place at the time, the National Labor Relations Board could hold a big brand jointly responsible when workers at its franchises or contractors were underpaid or blocked from unionizing, even if the brand only set the rules indirectly [S2]. This bill would make that much harder, letting corporations set the rules without sharing legal responsibility. It never advanced beyond a Senate committee hearing before the Congress ended [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Franchisors (fast-food chains, hotel brands), lead contractors, and other companies that set standards for franchisees and subcontractors gain the most: they would no longer be on the hook as joint employers for wage, union, and working-condition violations at businesses they do not directly run [S2][S3]. Workers at those locations would have a harder time organizing and bargaining with the large company that actually shapes their pay and conditions [S2].

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the National Labor Relations Act so that two or more employers count as 'joint employers' only if each shares and exercises actual, direct, and immediate control over essential terms and conditions of employment.

This would shield franchisors, lead contractors, and parent companies from being held jointly responsible for labor-law violations and union bargaining at franchised or subcontracted businesses they do not directly operate.

analysis.who_pays: Workers at franchised and subcontracted businesses would bear the cost: they could no longer bargain with or sue the large corporation that sets their conditions, leaving only the smaller local employer legally responsible. Unions lose a key organizing route [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: By requiring 'actual, direct, and immediate' control, the bill would let franchisors and lead firms keep setting the real terms of work while insulating themselves from labor-law responsibility, leaving workers with no bargaining partner with power over their conditions.

The bill would reverse the NLRB's 2015 joint-employer standard, which allowed responsibility to reach companies that indirectly control working conditions — the situation labor groups argued was necessary for franchise and subcontracted workers to organize effectively.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For franchisors and firms that outsource labor, the bill removes legal exposure for workers' pay and conditions at businesses they effectively control, at the cost of workers losing a deep-pocketed, accountable employer when their rights are violated. Supporters would say it restores a common-sense rule that only direct control counts; the cost is that workers at franchised or subcontracted workplaces can face a wall between them and whoever actually sets their conditions.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, placed on the Senate calendar, and got a Senate Small Business Committee hearing in June 2016, but no committee vote or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced March 15, 2016, and read twice and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar over the next two days.
The Senate Small Business and Entrepreneurship Committee held a hearing on June 16, 2016, but the record shows no markup, vote, or floor action afterward.
The bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, without either chamber passing it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Franchisors, staffing firms, and other companies that benefit from not being counted as joint employers are better off; workers at franchise and subcontracted workplaces gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Lamar Alexander
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and chaired the Senate committee (Health, Education, Labor and Pensions) with jurisdiction over labor law.

for.name: 46 Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including Majority Leader Mitch McConnell.

for.name: Senate Small Business and Entrepreneurship Committee
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill in June 2016 but took no further action.

sides.party_line_note: All 47 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrats signed on.

industries.industry: Franchisors and large chains (fast food, hotels, retail)
industries.note: The bill would limit their legal responsibility as 'joint employers' for labor conditions at franchised locations, reducing exposure to union bargaining and labor-law liability while keeping the franchise business model intact.
A stricter joint-employer test makes it easier to keep workers formally employed by smaller intermediaries, limiting the accountability of the companies that actually set the work.
Joint-employer status is a key route to bargaining with large corporations over franchise and contract workers; narrowing it removes a major organizing target.
